title: Pho Bo
kicker: Hanoi's dawn soup: a beef broth so clear and fragrant you could read a newspaper through it.
story: Pho is a broth with a noodle habit. Everything else — the rice noodles, the rare beef, the mountain of herbs — is a garnish on the real work: beef bones charred with ginger and onion, simmered for hours with star anise, cinnamon and clove until the kitchen smells like a Hanoi street at 6 a.m.

Clarity is the pride of a northern pho bo. Parboil the bones and rinse them — this single step removes the impurities that would cloud everything. Then the gentlest simmer, skimming, and never a boil. The finished broth should be amber, translucent, and so layered with spice that guests will demand to know your secret. The secret is four hours and a strainer.
fun_fact: Pho likely evolved from French colonial beef culture (pot-au-feu's bones-and-clear-broth logic) meeting Vietnamese rice noodles — the word itself may descend from 'feu'.

ingredients.note: knuckle and marrow bones, plus oxtail if you can

ingredients.item: raw beef sirloin or eye round

ingredients.note: Thai basil, cilantro, sawtooth herb if lucky, lime wedges, bean sprouts, sliced chili

steps.title: Parboil and rinse the bones
steps.text: Cover bones with water, boil hard 5 minutes — a gray scum rises. Dump everything, rinse bones under running water, scrub the pot. This unglamorous step is the entire secret of a clear broth.

steps.title: Char the aromatics
steps.text: Broil onion and ginger until blackened and soft, 15 minutes. Toast the dry spices in a pan until fragrant, then tie loosely in cheesecloth — a spice bag you can fish out.

steps.title: The long, quiet simmer
steps.text: Bones, brisket, charred aromatics, spice bag, 4 L water. Bring to a bare simmer and hold there — one bubble every couple of seconds — for 4 hours, skimming occasionally. Remove brisket at the 2.5-hour mark so it stays tender.

steps.title: Season at the end
steps.text: Strain the broth. Season with fish sauce and rock sugar — taste: it should be slightly over-seasoned, because noodles and herbs will dilute it in the bowl.

steps.title: Bowls, fast
steps.text: Soak/cook noodles, divide into bowls. Lay raw sirloin slices on the noodles, then pour the boiling broth over — the thin slices cook in the bowl. Add brisket slices. Guests top their own with herbs, sprouts, lime and chili.

steps.title: Serve with the herb mountain
steps.text: Do not stir the whole bowl into confusion — locals lift noodles, dip into the broth, sip broth between. The plate of herbs is part of the meal, not a garnish. Broth first, noodles second, everything third.

notes: Freeze the sirloin 30 minutes for paper-thin slicing with a normal knife.
Broth keeps 4 days refrigerated (skims solid) and freezes 3 months — one session makes several pho nights.
Instant pot shortcut: 1 hour at high pressure after parboiling. Purists will say nothing; the broth will know.

storage: Broth refrigerates 4 days / freezes 3 months. Assemble bowls fresh every time; noodles and herbs never live in the broth.

equipment.n: skim, then strain - a cloudy broth is a lost argument
freeze the eye round 30 minutes, slice paper-thin

facts.first_recorded: c. 1900–1910 — street stalls in Hanoi, with French colonial beef demand in the background
facts.name_means: Pronounced 'fuh?' — theories run from French feu (pot-au-feu) to the cry of vendors. Nobody knows. Slurp anyway.
facts.technique: Clarity above all: parboil, skim, char the aromatics
facts.season: Any — breakfast in Hanoi is 5 AM
facts.signature: Star anise, charred ginger, Thai basil on top
facts.serve_at: With the plate of herbs to build as you go
facts.pour: Jasmine tea, or a bia hoi if it is that hour

relations.cluster_note: Three answers to one question. Tokyo says soy and wheat; Hanoi says clarity and rice; your grandmother says chicken.
